title: All Rise…For What? Baseball, Conformity, and Violence in the USA
author: David Masciotra
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-4.32.15-PM-680x465.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/31/all-
risefor-what-baseball-conformity-and-violence-in-the-usa/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-4.32.15-PM-922x630.png)

Photo by [Taylor
Rooney](https://unsplash.com/@rooney?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

One of the glaring inconsistencies of American life is that the culture prides
itself on “individual freedom,” but insists on blind participation in
collective ritual. The inculcation of the conformist impulse begins early with
the daily recitation of the “pledge of allegiance” in classrooms, and in a
display of national arrested development, it continues with an almost
identical exercise before every sports event, where the national anthem plays
with expectation that everyone in the audience will dutifully rise from their
seats, remove their hats, and show great reverence for…what exactly? The flag,
as prevalent bumper stickers and t-shirts declare, “In America, we stand for
the flag”? The song itself, a largely tuneless paean to war? Military
veterans? When former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick took a knee during the
National Anthem to protest racial profiling and police brutality, he was
widely accused of “disrespecting the troops.” Or all of the above in a country
that has no real sense of shared culture or history?

It is doubtful that the most pious of patriots can coherently explain, but
they will get quite angry with those who refuse to participate. Much of
America functions as an inverse execution of psychoanalyst Erik Erikson’s
concept of “negative identity.” While Erikson coined the term to describe
malcontents who define themselves in perpetual opposition to social mores, in
America it is typical to identify in opposition to those who counter the
mainstream; who conflict with social mores. So, you don’t who you are, but you
know you aren’t the guy who doesn’t stand for the anthem. You don’t know what
it means to be “white,” but you know you aren’t Black. You don’t know what
“American values” really constitute, but you know they are not the same values
as the people we are bombing. To paraphrase the “Star Spangled Banner,” the
bombs are always bursting in air…somewhere.

I recently considered the oddity of American ritual when attending a Chicago
White Sox game with my father and uncle. My dad, who was drafted into the
Vietnam War, was in his seat when a voice over the sound system instructed all
attendees to “please rise for the National Anthem.” He later told me that he
remained seated, preferring to eat his hot dog in relative comfort. My uncle
and I were in the concession stand concourses. He was looking for Italian
sausage, while I was trying to find a beer vendor that sold Leinenkugel’s
Summer Shandy. Distracting me from my search for my beverage, preferably on
draft, was something that resembled a scene from a science fiction movie in
which the activation of some devious device places everyone into a catatonic
state. In the concession area, almost everyone stopped moving, paused their
business transactions, and fell silent to turn toward the field. Most held
their ballcaps over their chests. My eloquent reaction was to mutter, under my
breath, “what the fuck?” I continued walking, my own hat still squarely on my
head, as did my uncle, also wearing headgear. A few of the pious gave us dirty
looks. I wondered if anyone would confront us, perhaps even with an insult or
threat. The blood and hatred in the American air can always explode into
violence. In a country with 500 million civilian-owned guns, and concealed
carry liberties, including in the reliably “blue” Illinois, the explosion
often becomes literal, inside a victim’s stomach, chest, or cranial cavity.

Perhaps, too hypnotized by the patriotic spectacle, no one chastised my uncle
or me. He found his encased meat of choice, and I did locate the summer shandy
on draft for a plunderous $15.

Less than two weeks later, controversy, violence, and characteristic Americans
idiocy did ensue at a Chicago baseball game, only it was on the north side in
the storied, pastoral Wrigley Field. A [cell phone
video](https://www.nbcchicago.com/mlb/chicago-cubs/man-who-slapped-cubs-fan-
for-not-standing-during-national-anthem-speaks-out/3965062/) went viral, at
least in the Chicagoland area, of a twentysomething man remaining seated
during the National Anthem, while an elderly man behind him, wearing a Cubs
jersey customized to feature his own surname across the shoulders, barked at
him, “Stand up! Stand up!” When the young guy failed to respond, the angry old
man smacked him across the back of the head. With a look of shock on his face,
the young man slowly rose to his feet. Still not satisfied, the patriot, who
just committed an assault in front of hundreds of witnesses, none of whom did
a thing to respond, continued to shout toward the back of his victim’s head.

The assailant was later identified as Robert Chavez. In an interview with
“Inside Edition,” Chavez explained that security did intend to remove him from
the stadium, but his victim actually talked them out of it. Not only did he
cooperate with the slap and convince security to let the slapper enjoy the
game, he also bought Chavez a beer. The Chicago Cubs organization declined to
punish Chavez, and the local media treated the story with a tone of amusement.

In his interview, Chavez confessed to the crime with a degree of remorse,
[saying](https://www.nbcchicago.com/mlb/chicago-cubs/man-who-slapped-cubs-fan-
for-not-standing-during-national-anthem-speaks-out/3965062/), “Even though I
fought in Vietnam and I had buddies killed, you know, I mean, we fight for the
rights of the people, and that’s one of his rights.”

It leaves one punch-drunk to contemplate how over 51 years after the Fall of
Saigon, there are still Americans, combat veterans no less, who believe that
the Bill of Rights was somehow at stake in the jungles and villages of
Vietnam. Perhaps, it is a coping mechanism for Chavez, along with the many
Vietnam Vets who I see walking around grocery stores in sweatshirts and
baseball caps advertising their service, to believe that their “buddies were
killed” and that they themselves killed people to preserve the American “way
of life” against an existential threat; to protect the right of a young man,
five decades later, to sit or stand during the National Anthem. My father
doesn’t believe that absurdity nor do most of the veterans, like Tim O’Brien,
Robert Kovic, Larry Heinemann, and Lynda Van Devanter, who wrote the great
literature of the war. But it is sufficiently widespread that every Memorial
Day, Veteran’s Day, and Fourth of July includes celebrations of those fought
not only in Vietnam, but also Afghanistan and Iraq, whether it was the Gulf
War or the post-9/11 “weapons of mass destruction” monstrosity, as defenders
of “American freedom.”

Rare is acknowledgement of the [three million
Vietnamese](https://www.npr.org/2013/01/28/169076259/anything-that-moves-
civilians-and-the-vietnam-war) who the US annihilated or the millions who
remained to suffer the defects and diseases that result from agent orange
poisoning. It is uncommon to hear discussion of the American soldiers, like my
father, who have had a lifetime of health issues related to exposure to the
same chemical weaponry. There is hardly a passing thought for the Afghans and
Iraqis, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, who died in American wars.
Like their medical cousins in Vietnam, [thousands of
civilians](https://www.salon.com/2016/09/18/stack-the-bodies-outside-the-door-
pollution-contamination-and-the-toxic-legacy-of-the-iraq-war-on-the-iraqis-
themselves/) in those countries also deal with an assortment of maladies, some
of them life-threatening, from the environmental toxicity that lingers after
days and days and days of bullets, bombs, military pollution, and burn pits.

The end of the war is hardly the end of the torture and torment – not for the
civilians of the countries that our military leaves choking in the dust or for
the women and children who have to tiptoe around the traumatized, maladjusted,
on-edge man in their home. [Stacy
Bannerman](https://washingtonmonthly.com/2025/06/25/when-it-comes-to-military-
service-connected-domestic-violence-silence-is-deadly/), a heroic leader of
the campaign for military spouses and children, has dedicated much of her life
to spotlighting the dark corners of violence that few Americans, especially
those in positions of legal, political, or military leadership, are willing to
explore. She has testified in front of Congress that households with a combat
veteran are three to five times likelier to experience domestic violence. Her
research has also uncovered that the United States Army even has an
“acceptable rate of domestic violence,” meaning a rate that they find
manageable from a public relations and personnel management standpoint; a rate
that does not require or motivate an official response.

The war machine that is central to American power must silence consideration
of the lives that it crushes into the dirt. As Bruce Springsteen sings in
“Last to Die,”

> We don’t measure the blood we’ve drawn anymore  
>  We just stack the bodies outside the door…

Essential to the stacking is a religious reverence for America itself, turning
on the dogma that American wars – no matter how many revelations emerge
regarding real reasons and specious justifications – are about “freedom.” It
is not so much a historical argument or political analysis, but theological
doctrine. The young man who Robert Chavez slapped, whether he remained seated
as a protest or as an expression of laziness, was a heretic. Heretics deserve
punishment.

Sociologist Robert Bellah wrote in 1967 that the “theme” of American life is a
“continuous one in civil religion.” “From the earliest years of the republic
is a collection of beliefs, symbols, and rituals with respect to sacred things
and institutionalized in a collectivity,” Bellah asserted as part of his
explanation that there is “no other word” but “religion” to describe how most
Americans (I would add, white Americans), from the powerful to the one-out-of-
one-hundred-million voter, views their society.

Bellah was not entirely opposed to civil religion, as he believed that it
could promote social cohesion, civic virtue, and public service, but he did
write that the Vietnam War, the Watergate scandal, and the daily injustices
that the Civil Rights Movement had brought to the forefront, drained and
discarded much of the substance of the American religion, leaving only a
“broken and empty shell.”

The broken and empty shell provokes a massive investment of time and energy –
manpower, political resources, and cultural pressure – to make it appear
solid, robust, and expansive. White Americans, along with certain immigrant
groups attempting to assimilate according to the most obnoxious model of
mainstream behavior, love their flags, anthems, patriotic clothing, and
declarations of American superiority. Anyone who has lived abroad or travelled
to an educated, developed country can attest that the constant displays of
national pride in the US, which obviously mask deep feelings of insecurity,
are odd and novel. One is unlikely to hear an Italian declare that Italy is
the “greatest country in the history of the world.” It is difficult to imagine
a Japanese politician announcing, as Kamala Harris did about her own national
identity, that “the greatest privilege on Earth is being Japanese.”

I recall one of my first conversations with a Croatian immigrant in college.
She told me that when she arrived in the United States, she was “frightened”
by all the flags flying from every government building, many businesses, and
countless private homes. It reminded her of when the Croatian War of
Independence broke out during the 1990s, the only time she saw such widespread
and garish exhibitions of patriotism in a European country.

Of course, when she arrived in the US, the country was at war with two
countries, Afghanistan and Iraq, under the umbrella policy of the “war on
terror,” which would eventually lead to the bombing of eight additional
countries, and the deployment of special forces on missions in several African
nations. Even the least seasoned political observer can make a safe bet that,
irrespective of the president, political party in power, or domestic
circumstances, the US is bombing some foreign city. Unless the bombing
campaign qualifies as a “war,” as is the current policy toward Iran, the
“death from above” method of international relations is not even subject to
debate. In the first year of his second term in office, Donald Trump has
authorized the bombings of seven countries: Iraq, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia,
Syria, Venezuela, and Yemen. What percentage of Americans could name these
countries? What percentage of journalists, for that matter?

Most Americans don’t know who their government is bombing, or why, but they
will stand for the National Anthem at the nearest sporting event. Surveys show
that Generation Z is less patriotic than their forebears, with [56
percent](https://www.newsweek.com/us-gen-z-young-millennials-patriotic-older-
generations-poll-11939631) of them telling national pollsters that they are
“proud to be American” (Generation X and Baby Boomers score higher). Well over
half is still a strong showing for Gen Z, and the number could easily rise
when the ghastly Donald Trump is no longer in office. I was recently surprised
at a Fourth of July party to see the large number of recent college graduates
wearing patriotic-themed clothing. A few of them asked my wife and me why we
weren’t wearing “red, white and blue.”

On the same day, I saw footage of [Barack
Obama](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/EjrHHxI_4wQ) explain that, even though
George Washington owned slaves, it “does not negate his greatness.” Such a
baffling statement is similar to declaring that Charles Manson was a good
musician. The whole murderous cult thing doesn’t “negate his greatness.”

Arguing that keeping human beings as property isn’t a profound enough failure
to condemn a leader makes as much sense as young people displaying national
pride or smacking young people who refuse to display national pride in a
country that is currently rounding up minorities, encaging them in abusive and
filthy conditions, and killing those who protest in the streets. For those not
under the hypnosis of devotional zeal, it is challenging to have pride in a
country that allows thousands of people to die each year for lack of health
care coverage, while many more suffer financial ruin due to “medical debt.”
One of our national hymns is “America the Beautiful,” and yet with each
passing day, more of our natural beauty faces destruction at the hands of
corporate machinery and relaxed pollution standards, destroying wildlife
habitats, threatening livable ecology, and allowing the degradation of natural
treasures from the Alaskan wild to the Indiana Dunes.

But just as it would be improper to walk into a prayer meeting with questions
about epistemology, one doesn’t poke at a civil religion. In reviewing the
career of Robert Bellah, historian [Ray
Haberski](https://s-usih.org/2013/08/robert-bellahs-legacy-and-a-lingering-
question/) concludes that the deep moral transformation that genuine leaders,
like Martin Luther King, hoped to achieve is unlikely. Instead, periods of
reform will merely smooth the rough edges to renew the faith. “The United
States [is] is too big to fail,” Haberski writes.

His Great Recession lingo is appropriate. The US is one giant bubble, waiting
to pop. The instinct to smack a young guy who sits during the anthem is a
milder version of the imperative that a masked agent of the state feels when
shooting a protestor: Anything to keep the thin surface intact.

Conformity and violence? As American as baseball and apple pie.
